title: Mencius: The Child at the Well and the Ox
bigQuestion: How does Mencius argue that people have the beginnings of goodness, and what did he think that meant for rulers?

story.title: The Trembling Ox
story.kicker: A king sees an ox being led to sacrifice, and he cannot bear it.
paragraphs: The scene comes from the Mencius, book 1A, chapter 7. King Xuan of Qi, a powerful ruler of the Warring States period, is sitting in his hall. Servants lead an ox past him. The ox is on its way to be killed, so its blood can be used to consecrate a new bell.

The king sees the animal trembling. He tells the servants to let it go. They ask whether the ceremony should be dropped. No, the king says. Use a sheep instead. Later the people of Qi gossip. They say the king was being stingy, swapping a big animal for a small one.

Mencius, a traveling teacher, hears the story and visits the king. He says he does not think the king was stingy. He says the king saw the ox and did not see the sheep. What moved him was a feeling that could not bear the ox's fear. Mencius tells the king that this feeling is enough to rule well.

The king is pleased and puzzled. If he has this feeling, why are his people suffering? Mencius's answer is the heart of the chapter. The king has the feeling. He has not yet carried it from the ox to his own people. The rest of the conversation is about how to carry it that far.
story.think: Mencius says the king's pity for one ox proves he could rule kindly. Is that a fair step? What would the king need to do next?

lessons.title: The Second Sage
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius was a Confucian teacher of the fourth century BCE, later honored as the "Second Sage" after Confucius.
reading: Mencius is the Latin form of Mengzi, "Master Meng." Legge spells it Mang-tsze in the older system. He lived about a century after Confucius, traditionally c. 372–289 BCE, though scholars note the dates are uncertain. He traveled between the courts of the Warring States, trying to persuade kings to rule humanely.

The book named after him, the *Mencius*, has seven books. Each book is split into two parts, A and B. So 2A.6 means book 2, part A, chapter 6. Most of the book is dialogue: Mencius talking with kings, students and rival thinkers. It reads more like a set of debates than a list of sayings.

Later Confucians gave Mencius great honor. Zhu Xi, in the 1100s, placed the Mencius among the Four Books, the core texts for study and, from 1313, for the state exams. Mencius became known as the Yasheng, the "Second Sage." Some readers today call his teachings the most hopeful in the Confucian tradition.

words.d: Mengzi, "Master Meng" (c. 372–289 BCE, dates uncertain); also the book of his teachings
the Analects, Mencius, Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean, grouped by Zhu Xi
a written conversation between two or more speakers

lessons.title: Arguing by Analogy
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius often argues by analogy, comparing human nature to water, sprouts or a mountain's trees.
reading: Mencius loved comparisons. He compared human nature to water that flows downhill, to sprouts that need care, and to a mountain whose trees were cut down. An *analogy* explains an unfamiliar thing by pointing to a familiar one. Mencius used analogies both to teach and to win debates.

One famous example is the Ox Mountain story in 6A.8. The mountain was once covered in trees. People cut them, and cattle grazed on the new shoots, so it looks bare. Mencius says people might think the mountain never had trees. In the same way, a person whose good feelings are cut back might seem to have none.

Analogies have limits, and Mencius's rivals pointed them out. A reader can test an analogy by asking where the two things are alike and where they differ. This course calls that *testing an analogy*. It is a key skill for reading Mencius, whose arguments often stand or fall on a comparison.

words.d: a comparison that explains one thing by pointing to another like it
the bare mountain in Mencius 6A.8, used as an analogy for human goodness cut back
asking where two compared things are alike and where they differ

look.title: Ox Mountain

look.prompt: What stands for human goodness in this analogy? What stands for the axes and cattle? Where might the analogy break down?

check.q: What happened to the trees in the Ox Mountain story?
choices: They grew into a great forest
They were planted by a king
They were cut, and cattle ate the new shoots
check.why: In 6A.8 axes and grazing cattle left the mountain bare.

check.q: What does the bare mountain stand for, in Mencius's analogy?
choices: A person whose good feelings have been cut back
check.why: Mencius says a person may seem to lack goodness because it has been cut back, like the trees.

check.q: How can a reader test an analogy?

check.why: Testing an analogy means checking likenesses and differences.

lessons.title: Legge's Mencius
lessons.mainIdea: Legge's translation of the Mencius, first published in 1861 and revised in 1895, is public domain and can be quoted exactly.
reading: James Legge published The Works of Mencius as volume 2 of The Chinese Classics in 1861. A second, revised edition appeared in 1895. Like his Analects, it prints the Chinese text, Legge's English and long notes. His notes often explain Chinese commentators, especially Zhu Xi.

Legge admired Mencius, but he also argued with him. In his introduction he questioned Mencius's claim that human nature is good, from the point of view of his own Christian beliefs about human nature. Readers today can see both his care as a translator and the views he brought to the text.

Legge's English uses some words that need a gloss. "Benevolence" is ren. "Righteousness" is *yi*. "Propriety" is li. "Knowledge" or "wisdom" is *zhi*. "Principle" in 2A.6 translates duan, a sprout or starting point. Knowing these helps a reader see the Chinese terms behind the English.

words.d: righteousness; what is right or fitting; Legge writes "righteousness"
wisdom or knowledge; knowing right from wrong
a sprout or starting point; Legge writes "principle" in Mencius 2A.6

look.title: Principle or Sprout?
look.text: Legge (1895) writes that the feeling of commiseration is "the principle of benevolence." Many modern translators write "the sprout" or "the beginning" of benevolence for the same Chinese word, duan.
look.prompt: How does "sprout" change the picture compared with "principle"? What does a sprout need that a principle does not?

check.q: In which year did Legge publish his revised Works of Mencius?
check.why: The first edition was 1861; the revised second edition was 1895.

check.q: What does duan mean, the word Legge renders "principle" in 2A.6?
check.why: Duan is a sprout or beginning; many modern translators write "sprout."

check.q: What did Legge question in his introduction to the Mencius?
choices: Mencius's claim that human nature is good
The number of books in the Mencius
check.why: Legge questioned it from his own Christian view of human nature.

lessons.title: A Mind That Cannot Bear
lessons.mainIdea: In Mencius 2A.6, Mencius says everyone has a heart that cannot bear to see others suffer, shown by the alarm anyone feels at a child about to fall into a well.
reading: Mencius 2A.6 begins with a claim. Legge: "All men have a mind which cannot bear to see the sufferings of others." Then Mencius gives a test case. "If men suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they will without exception experience a feeling of alarm and distress."

Mencius is careful about the reason. The feeling does not come, he says, from wanting to win the favor of the child's parents. It does not come from wanting praise from neighbors and friends. It does not come from disliking the sound of the child's cry. It comes first, before any of these reasons.

This is a *thought experiment*: an imagined case used to test an idea. Mencius does not say everyone will save the child. He says everyone will feel the jolt. The feeling is the starting point. Readers still debate whether the example shows what Mencius claims, and use it in modern discussions of empathy.

words.d: an imagined case used to test an idea
Legge's word for feeling pity or sorrow for another's suffering
sharing or understanding another person's feelings

look.cite: The Works of Mencius 2A.6, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1895
look.prompt: Why does Mencius say "suddenly"? What would change if the person had time to think first?

check.q: What does Mencius say anyone would feel on suddenly seeing a child about to fall into a well?

check.q: Which reason for the feeling does Mencius rule out?

check.q: What is a thought experiment?

lessons.title: The Four Sprouts
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius 2A.6 names four feelings as the beginnings of the four virtues: benevolence, righteousness, propriety and wisdom.
reading: After the child at the well, Mencius lists four feelings. Legge: "The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence. The feeling of shame and dislike is the principle of righteousness. The feeling of modesty and complaisance is the principle of propriety. The feeling of approving and disapproving is the principle of knowledge."

The four virtues are ren, yi, li and zhi. Each grows from a feeling. Mencius then compares them to the body: "Men have these four principles just as they have their four limbs." A person without them, he says, would hardly be human. Readers call these the *four sprouts*.

A sprout is small. It needs care or it dies. Mencius says the four beginnings must be developed, like a fire just lit or a spring just flowing. This is the core of his view that human nature is good. He means people start with good tendencies, not that everyone already acts well.

words.d: Mencius's four feelings that are beginnings of ren, yi, li and zhi
Legge's word for yielding politely to others
a good quality of character developed over time

check.q: What does Mencius mean by saying human nature is good?

lessons.title: Willow and Water
lessons.mainIdea: In Mencius 6A.1–2 Mencius debates Gaozi, who compares human nature to willow wood and to water that can flow either way.
reading: Gaozi was a thinker who debated Mencius. In 6A.1 he says human nature is like willow wood, and righteousness is like cups and bowls carved from it. Goodness, in this view, is shaped from outside. Mencius replies that carving a willow into bowls does violence to the tree. Would goodness then do violence to people?

In 6A.2 Gaozi tries water. Nature is like water swirling in a pool, he says. Open it east and it flows east; open it west and it flows west. So nature is neither good nor bad. Mencius turns the analogy around. Legge: "The tendency of man's nature to good is like the tendency of water to flow downwards."

This is a *rebuttal*: an answer that turns an opponent's point back on them. Mencius accepts water as the image, then argues it shows a direction after all. Readers ask who wins. Some say Mencius only changed the subject from east and west to up and down. Others find his move convincing.

words.d: a thinker who debated Mencius about human nature in Mencius book 6A
an answer that argues against an opponent's point
what people are like from birth, before training

look.title: Water Flows Downward
look.text: The tendency of man's nature to good is like the tendency of water to flow downwards. There are none but have this tendency to good, just as all water flows downwards.
look.cite: The Works of Mencius 6A.2, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1895
look.prompt: Gaozi said water flows east or west. Mencius says it flows down. Did Mencius answer Gaozi's point, or change it?

check.q: What did Gaozi compare human nature to in 6A.1?
check.why: Gaozi compared nature to willow and righteousness to cups and bowls.

check.q: How did Mencius use Gaozi's water analogy in 6A.2?
choices: He said water still tends to flow downward, as nature tends to good

check.why: Mencius turned the image: nature tends to good as water tends downward.

check.q: What is a rebuttal?
choices: An answer that argues against an opponent's point
check.why: Mencius's water reply is a rebuttal of Gaozi.

lessons.title: From the Ox to the People
lessons.mainIdea: In Mencius 1A.7 Mencius uses King Xuan's pity for an ox to argue that the king could extend kindness to his people.
reading: In Mencius 1A.7 King Xuan spares a trembling ox and orders a sheep used instead. The people call him stingy. Mencius says the king saw the ox and did not see the sheep. His heart was moved by what was in front of him. Mencius calls this the working of benevolence.

Then Mencius makes his key move. He says the king's kindness reaches animals but not his people. The problem is not that the king cannot. It is that he does not. Mencius compares it to someone who says he cannot lift a feather, when he simply does not try. The king must *extend* his feeling.

To extend means to carry something outward. Mencius urges the king to treat other people's elders as he treats his own, and others' children as his own. Readers see this as a plan for humane rule built from one small moment of feeling. Critics ask whether feeling alone is enough to guide a state.

words.d: to carry a feeling or practice outward, from near to far
the ruler in Mencius 1A.7 who spares an ox from sacrifice
Mencius's term for rule that cares for the people's needs

look.title: The King and the Ox

look.prompt: Why does Mencius start with the king's own feeling instead of giving him rules? What must the king do next?

check.q: Why does Mencius say the king spared the ox and not the sheep?

check.q: What does Mencius urge the king to do with his feeling?
check.why: Mencius asks the king to carry his kindness outward to his people.

lessons.title: The People Come First
lessons.mainIdea: In Mencius 7B.14 Mencius ranks the people as most important, the spirits of land and grain next, and the ruler last.
reading: Mencius 7B.14 is short and bold. Legge: "The people are the most important element in a nation; the spirits of the land and grain are the next; the sovereign is the lightest." The spirits of land and grain were honored at state altars. They stood for the state itself.

In a world of kings, this ranking was striking. Mencius goes on to say that a ruler who endangers the altars can be replaced. Elsewhere, in 1B.8, he says that a tyrant who destroys goodness has lost the right to be called a ruler. These passages link to the older idea of the *Mandate of Heaven*.

The Mandate of Heaven was the belief, older than Confucius, that Heaven grants the right to rule to a worthy ruler and can withdraw it. Mencius said Heaven sees as the people see. Later rulers were not always pleased. The first Ming emperor had an edition of the Mencius printed with dozens of passages cut out, though the full text was later restored.

words.d: the belief that Heaven grants the right to rule to worthy rulers and can take it away
a king or ruler
a cruel ruler who harms the people

lessons.title: Mencius and Xunzi
lessons.mainIdea: Xunzi, a later Confucian, argued that human nature is bad and goodness comes from teaching and ritual, directly challenging Mencius.
reading: Xunzi was a Confucian thinker of the third century BCE. In the chapter often called "Human Nature Is Bad," chapter 23 of the Xunzi, he argues against Mencius by name. People are born, he says, wanting gain and feeling envy. Left alone, they fight. Goodness comes from teachers, ritual and effort.

Xunzi uses his own analogies. A warped board must be steamed and pressed to become straight. Metal must be ground to become sharp. So people need li and learning to become good. Where Mencius sees sprouts that need care, Xunzi sees crooked wood that needs shaping.

Both men were Confucians. Both valued learning and ritual. They disagreed about the starting point. Later tradition, especially after Zhu Xi, sided with Mencius, and Xunzi was read less for centuries. Many scholars today study Xunzi closely again. They present the two as a real debate *within* the tradition.

words.d: a Confucian thinker (3rd century BCE) who argued human nature is bad; also his book
set forms of action, like ceremonies and manners; li
among thinkers who share the same school

look.title: Sprout or Warped Board?

look.prompt: Both men say people need learning. What is the real difference between the two images?

It is good, like water flowing down
It is the same as the Dao
check.why: Xunzi's chapter 23 argues human nature is bad.

check.q: What image did Xunzi use for shaping people?
choices: A warped board steamed and pressed straight
check.why: Xunzi compared people to warped wood that must be straightened.

check.q: How does the lesson describe the Mencius-Xunzi disagreement?
choices: A war between Daoists and Confucians

check.why: Both were Confucians who disagreed about the starting point of human nature.

lessons.title: Mencius Among His Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Readers have used Mencius in many ways, from exam study to arguments about rulers' duties to modern debates on human rights and empathy.
reading: For centuries, students memorized the Mencius for the state exams. They learned 2A.6 and 7B.14 by heart. Zhu Xi's notes shaped how they read it. For many families, knowing Mencius well was a path to office and honor. Only men could sit the exams, and most candidates never passed.

Other readers used Mencius to criticize rulers. Scholars pointed to 7B.14 when rulers failed the people. In Korea and Japan too, Mencius was read, argued over and sometimes feared for his ideas about replacing bad rulers. In the twentieth century some writers linked Mencius to democracy. Others warned that his ideas are not the same as modern democracy.

Today, philosophers and psychologists sometimes cite the child at the well in discussions of empathy and moral feeling. Some Confucian revivalists see Mencius as the heart of the tradition. Some critics find his optimism too simple. A careful reader can describe all these uses and still return to the text itself.

words.d: a hopeful view that things are or can become good
someone who works to bring an older tradition back into wide use
the state tests, based on the classics, used for centuries to choose Chinese officials
